Christopher Beck, M.Sc. · Dr. Francesco Vona · Prof. Stefan Albertz

Hello

Christopher Beck, M.Sc. Lecturer at Hochschule Hamm-Lippstadt. Co-lecturers: Dr. Francesco Vona and Prof. Stefan Albertz.

Why I give this course

  • I like explaining things until they click.
  • Sound and images are everywhere. Few people see how they work inside.
  • I want this room to feel like a place where you like to be.

No Need to Fear

"I cannot program"

I do not expect you to learn Python. In the practicum you sometimes run cells in a notebook and change numbers. That is all.

"Too much math"

Formulas are hidden by default (key M). We try first, calculate later. Small calculations only.

"A tricky exam"

Written, multiple choice, 90 minutes. Three core topics per lecture. You get a practice trainer.

"I missed a week"

All slides, the notebooks of the practicum and the knowledge graph are online. Each lecture starts with a short recap.

"I have no audio background"

Good. We start from zero: what is a dB, what is a sample. Every new word is explained once.

"I will look silly"

Everybody here started at zero, me included. Nobody is judged on what they do not know yet.

Three Building Blocks

The whole semester rests on three foundations.

30 to 40 %

Audio

Measuring sound, digital audio, loudspeakers, filters, FFT and loudness.

30 to 40 %

Image and video

Cameras, color, scopes, displays and video compression.

Perception and efficiency

How we hear and see, and how that keeps file sizes small.

The third block connects the first two: knowing the ear and the eye tells us what we can leave out.

Interactive Slides and Notebooks

Some topics click only when you hear or see them change. This deck has interactive elements for that. When we implement something in code, we mostly use Jupyter notebooks.

1 · Run

Press play on a cell. A sound or an image appears.

→

2 · Change

Change one number: the sample rate, the filter, the bit depth.

→

3 · Notice

Run again. You hear or see what changed. The idea sticks.

When it is worth it

Where the lecture content really clicks once you play with it: aliasing, filters, spectra, color.

When we skip it

Some topics are better as a talk or a derivation. A notebook there would be dry, so there is none.

The course itself is built from interactive slides, not from notebooks. Where we write code, we use Jupyter notebooks in the browser. Code is a means, not the goal.

Every Day

Hearing aid

A tiny computer. It splits sound into bands, makes quiet parts louder, removes noise, and must be fast: a delay of a few milliseconds is already annoying.

Zoom, Webex, Teams

Your voice is sampled, compressed, sent, and rebuilt. Echo is removed. Video is compressed with the same ideas we meet in lecture 13.

Self-driving car

Cameras see color and brightness. Ultrasonic sensors measure distance with sound echoes. Both are signals that must be processed first.

Thinking Across Fields

This course combines interdisciplinary thinking and systems thinking, the way your third semester asks for it.

Interdisciplinary

Physics, signals, perception and engineering meet in one topic.

Systems thinking

A microphone, a codec and an ear are one chain. Change one link and the rest reacts.

I hope you come to enjoy diving deeper and interconnecting what you know.

Why This Course?

Three Domains: Air, Wire, Numbers

Sound travels through three worlds. We measure it differently in each.

AcousticsAirSound pressure p in pascal (Pa).
Level in dB SPL.
Reference: 20 µPa
→
AnalogueWireVoltage U in volt (V).
Level in dBu or dBV.
Reference: 0.775 V or 1 V
→
DigitalNumbersSamples with N bits.
Level in dBFS.
Reference: full scale

Microphone: air → wire. A/D converter: wire → numbers. And back: D/A converter, then loudspeaker.

Same idea in all three: a level in dB is a ratio to a reference. Always ask: relative to what?

EXAM

Why Everything Depends on Frequency

One idea explains most of audio: a sound wave has a length, and things have a size.

1.0 kHz
Wavelength in air

Axis: frequency (grey) and wavelength in air (teal). Bass, mids and highs are pink noise in that band (20–250 Hz, 250 Hz–4 kHz, 4–16 kHz). Laptop speakers play little below 100 Hz. Use headphones.

ThingSizeWhat the sound does

Reason 1 · Size against wavelength

Long waves bend around small things. Short waves are blocked or sent in one direction. Bass is everywhere in the room. Treble stays in front of the speaker.

Reason 2 · Things are slow

A membrane, a wall or a circuit has mass and springiness. It follows slow changes, but not fast ones, or it rings at its own favourite frequency.

Every device has a different gain at every frequency. That is the frequency response.

Every dB Is a Ratio

dBFS
below the digital maximum
dB SPL
relative to the quietest audible sound
dBu
relative to 0.775 volt
+6 dB
Voltage (pressure) isPower is

+6 dB: voltage twice as big.
+3 dB: power twice as big.
+20 dB: voltage ten times as big.

dB = 20·log₁₀(U₂/U₁) = 10·log₁₀(P₂/P₁)

U voltage, P power. Power grows with the square of the voltage, so the factor is 20 instead of 10.

Weighting curves after IEC 61672. Z is flat (no weighting). All are 0 dB at 1 kHz. A follows the ear at quiet levels, C is nearly flat.

Digital audio

Digital Audio: Three Numbers

Sampling rate

How often do we measure per second?

Samples per second.
Sets the highest frequency we can store.

Bit depth

How much dynamic range do we need?

Bits per sample.
Sets the noise floor and the dynamic range.

Buffer

How long does the digital version need from input to output?

Samples per block.
Sets the delay (latency).

Next: one slide for each number. A converter does the step from voltage to numbers.

EXAM

Sampling: How Often Do We Measure per Second?

Teal: the tone we want. Dots: the samples. Amber: the tone the samples really describe.

3.0 kHz
Highest safe toneStored as

Highest safe tone = half the sampling rate. Above it, tones fold back down.

f_stored = |f − k·f_s|, k whole number

EXAM

Bit Depth: How Much Dynamic Range?

3
StepsDynamic range

Top: the signal (teal) and its rounded version (amber). Bottom: the rounding error. We hear it as noise.

Each extra bit gives about 6 dB more dynamic range.

DR ≈ 6.02·N + 1.76 dB

N bits per sample, DR dynamic range of a full-scale sine against the rounding noise.

EXAM

Buffer: How Long From Input to Output?

Hear the delay · speech-like syllables plus a delayed copy

10 ms: the sound gets a metallic color. 50 ms: it sounds doubled. 100 ms: a clear echo.

Reading: Wessel & Wright (2002), Computer Music Journal 26(3): musical control wants latency below 10 ms. Haas (1951), Acustica 1: delays above about 30–50 ms are heard as a separate echo.

256
One buffer takesRound trip

Round trip ≈ 2 buffers + about 3 ms for the converters.
Small buffer: low delay, but the computer has little time. Large buffer: safe, but late.

t = B / f_s  ·  round trip ≈ 2·B / f_s + 3 ms

B buffer size in samples, f_s sampling rate.

EXAM

Take-Home Message

dB

A dB is a ratio. Always ask: relative to what?
+6 dB voltage ×2 · +3 dB power ×2

Clipping

0 dBFS is a wall. Keep headroom.

Sampling and bits

Rate: highest tone = half the rate.
Bits: about 6 dB per bit.

Buffer

Small buffer: low delay, little time. Large buffer: late, but safe.

Why Do DAWs Calculate in Float? Start Simple

One singer is one track. A concert is hundreds. The mix adds them all.

TracksPeak of the sum16-bit integerFloat

Why Do DAWs Calculate in Float?

Problem 1 · The mix gets too loud inside

You add tracks to a mix. Each peaks at −12 dBFS.

8
Worst-case peak of the sum16-bit integerFloat

In integer, the sum is cut at 0 dBFS in the middle of the chain and the loss stays. In float, you lower the master fader at the end and nothing is lost.

Identical tracks add their pressure: 20·log₁₀(N) dB. Different tracks add less (10·log₁₀ N dB).

Problem 2 · The recording was too quiet

You forgot the gain. Later you boost the file by the missing amount.

−60 dBFS
Steps left in 16-bit integerFloat keeps24 bit of detail

Integer has a fixed step size. A quiet signal uses only a few steps and sounds rough after boosting. Float stores a value and a scale, so a quiet signal keeps its fine detail.

Float32: 1 sign bit, 8 exponent bits, 23 mantissa bits (24 significant bits).

EXAM

32-bit Float: Headroom Only Inside the DAW

Red dashed: ±1 = 0 dBFS. Left: float value inside the DAW. Right: what the converter can output.

+12 dB
Peak inside the DAWPeak at the converter

Float32 keeps 24 bit mantissa + 8 bit exponent: values above ±1 are stored and can be scaled back. The converter has a hard wall at ±1.

Data Rate: How Much Data per Minute?

Data per second = samples per second × bits per sample × channels.

R = fs · N · C
Bit rate RBytes per secondPer minutePer hour

R data rate (bit/s) · fs sampling rate (Hz) · N bits per sample · C channels. 1 byte = 8 bit.

2

EXAM

Recording Over a Playback Track

Photo: singer with headphonesUnsplash: "recording studio headphones vocals"Click to add a picture

The singer hears the backing track and is recorded at the same time.

Two streams at once

Playback: computer → headphones.
Recording: microphone → computer.
Both run on a hardware clock. The clock never waits.

The computer works in blocks

It is called every few milliseconds and handles one block. A ring buffer sits between the clock and the program.

For computer scientists

It is a circular queue with one writer and one reader. No locks:

buf[w % L] = x;  w++;   // writer
x = buf[r % L];  r++;   // reader
fill = w - r;           // 0 … L

Ring Buffer: Recording and Playback

4
Fill levelDelay (fill ÷ clock)UnderrunsOverruns

Optimal: the fill stays between one block and L minus one block. The hardware side runs steady. The program works in blocks, like a bucket brigade.

L = 16 slots · w write pointer · r read pointer · after every access: index + 1 modulo L. Delay = fill ÷ hardware rate: a bigger fill is safer and later.

Break: 5 Minutes

5:00

Stretch. Question for the break: where does latency come from in your own setup?

Buffers: Latency Against Callback Deadline

Illustrative model: CPU load = overhead per callback / buffer time + processing share. Not a measurement.

256
40 %
Callback deadline B / fsRound trip 2B / fs + 3 msCPU load

The computer must finish each block before the next one is due. If it is late, you hear a click.

Adding Sources: +3 dB or +6 dB?

N equal sources24816
Different signals, 10·log₁₀ N+3.0+6.0+9.0+12.0
Identical, in phase, 20·log₁₀ N+6.0+12.0+18.1+24.1

Hear it

Different: two separate noises. Identical: one 440 Hz sine twice, B shifted by φ. At 180° it goes silent. Use headphones.

80 dB
80 dB
0°
SumOver the louder source

Different signals (two voices): +3 dB for two equal sources.
Identical signals: +6 dB. Opposite signals cancel.

L level (dB) · different signals: powers add · identical: pressures add with phase φ; φ = 180° cancels equal sources.

Phase: When Two Waves Meet

500 Hz
1.0 ms
Phase shift φSum compared with A

Same wave, shifted by half a period: silence. 343 m/s means 1 ms is 34 cm of path.

φ = 360° · f · Δt. Two speakers with the same signal at different distances give peaks and notches (comb filter).

Free field, point source. Each dot: one doubling of distance, −6.02 dB.

90 dB SPL

Double the distance: −6 dB.
Ten times the distance: −20 dB.

      After Today You Can …

      1. explain how a loudspeaker turns a current into sound, and why it needs a box and a crossover

      New Words Today

      Words from Lectures 1 and 2 you already know. These are new. Click a word.

      Recap of Lecture 2: Three Quick Questions

      From an Ideal Point Source to a Real System

      The ideal: a point source

      The real one: several drivers in a box

      Why more than one driver? Each size works in one range.

      Big cone: lots of air, but slow and beaming at the top. Small cone: fast, but too little air for bass.

      Wavelength and Size

      λ = c / f. Whenever an object is smaller than the wavelength, sound flows around it. When it is larger, it matters.

      Driver

      Lows spread, highs beam: the driver is small against low, large against high waves.

      Box

      Front and back cancel when the box is small against λ. That is why we need a box.

      Several sources

      Close against λ they couple, far apart they interfere. Lines and subwoofers.

      Warm-up: How Fast Is Sound?

      c ≈ 331.3 + 0.606 · T

      c in m/s, T in °C, dry air. About +0.6 m/s per degree.

      c = √(γ · R · T / M)

      Exact form, T in kelvin. Humid air is lighter: water vapour (M = 18) replaces nitrogen and oxygen (M = 29). So sound gets a little faster, about +0.4 % at 20 °C and 100 % humidity.

      t = d / c,   λ = c / f
      Speed of sound cSimple formula, dryTravel time t

      Sanity check: sound travels about 1 m in 3 ms, and 340 m in 1 s. Temperature matters (about 0.2 % per °C), humidity only a little.

      Warm-up: How Long Is the Wave?

      Guess first. Play the tone, type your guess in metres, press Check: you only hear if you are close, too small or too large. Then calculate λ = c / f, and press Solution only when you want to see it. Using .

      50 Hz
      100 Hz
      200 Hz
      400 Hz
      800 Hz
      8000 Hz

      Sanity checks: λ · f must give about 340. Double the frequency, half the wavelength. 1 kHz is about 34 cm. Is the size plausible for a room, a person, a hand?

      Low tones are hard to hear on laptop speakers: use headphones, with low volume.

      A Driver Is a Microphone in Reverse

      Current in the coil→force in the magnet field→cone moves→air pressure
      26 Hz
      70 %

      Equal loudness means equal air pressure. A low tone moves little air per stroke, so the cone must travel far: every time the frequency halves, the stroke grows 4 times. Untick the box to give every tone the same stroke instead.

      EXAM

      What the Air Does in a Lecture Hall

      100 Hz
      Seen on screen
      Level
      Wavelength

      Amber: squeezed air. Teal: stretched air. The red dot is one molecule: it only swings around its place. The wave travels, the air does not (real swing at 94 dB SPL, 100 Hz: about 4 µm). With a second speaker, the strip on top shows speaker 1 (dashed amber), speaker 2 (dashed teal, shifted by the chosen phase) and their sum (solid).

      Why a Box? Front and Back Cancel

      Schematic curves for the same driver. Shape matters, exact numbers do not.

      Without a box, the back wave of the cone meets the front wave and cancels the low notes.

      EXAM

      Two Drivers, One Crossover

      2.0 kHz

      The woofer plays the lows, the tweeter the highs. At the crossover frequency both play at −6 dB. Together they add up to a flat line.

      EXAM

      Headphones: Small Drivers, No Room

      Closed-back

      Seals the ear. Blocks outside noise. Good bass.

      Open-back

      Sound passes through. Airy, natural. Leaks to others.

      In-ear

      A tiny driver in the ear canal. Level depends on the fit.

      Impedance in ohms

      Common: 16–32 Ω (phones, in-ear), 80–250 Ω (studio), 600 Ω (high-end). Higher ohms need more voltage. A phone may be too weak.

      Mono and stereo

      Mono: the same signal in both ears. It sounds in the middle of the head. Stereo: the ears get different signals.

      HRTF: a hint

      Head and ears change every sound from every direction. Headphones skip this. Binaural audio puts it back. Lecture 4.

      Each ear gets only its own channel. There is no room and no crosstalk between the ears.
      Noise cancelling is a special case: a microphone and an inverted wave. See the next slide.

      EXAM

      Noise Cancelling: Add the Opposite Wave

      200 Hz
      0.0 ms
      0 dB
      Noise left

      Microphone → flip → play. Works best for low, steady noise.

      Speaker Layouts: Stereo, 5.1, Atmos

      60°

      Speakers and listener form an equilateral triangle: the speakers are as far apart as they are far from you. The angle is 60°.

      When the wavelength is bigger than the driver, the sound goes everywhere. When it is smaller, the driver beams the sound forward.

      The Problem: Front Row Loud, Back Row Quiet

      8 m
      Near field ends atLevel at 4 m, pointLevel at 4 m, line

      One speaker loses 6 dB per doubling of the distance: 5 m to 40 m is 18 dB. A line of speakers loses only 3 dB per doubling while you are close (near field). That evens out front and back. Next: how a line forms a beam, and how we aim it.

      Photo: line arrayClick to add a picture

      In front, all sources add in phase. At the sides they cancel. A small delay from source to source tilts the beam.

      Outlook: Signal Path of a 3-Way

      Active: filters before the amplifiers, one amplifier per driver (above). Passive: one amplifier, the filters sit behind it inside the box. f1 and f2 are the crossover frequencies.

      Take-Home Message

      Driver and box

      A driver moves air. A box stops front and back from cancelling.

      Crossover

      Each driver plays its own range. Polarity must be right.

      Datasheet

      A range needs a tolerance. Sensitivity: +3 dB per double power, −6 dB per double distance.

      Ears and directivity

      Every +3 dB halves the safe time. Highs beam, lows spread.

      Today

      The ear, Loudness, Masking, Directional hearing, Dynamics

      The Ear: Three Stages

      → →

      Air pressure → eardrum motion → fluid wave → nerve signal. Each stage changes the sound a little.

      EXAM

      The Cochlea: Place Is Frequency

      Equal steps along the cochlea mean equal frequency ratios. The ear measures pitch on a log scale, like dB.

      1.0 kHz
      Place from the oval window

      High notes excite the start of the cochlea. Low notes travel to the far end (the apex).

      Greenwood map: f = 165.4·(10^(2.1·x) − 0.88), x = share of the length measured from the apex.

      EXAM

      The Hearing Area (Hörfläche)

      1.0 kHz
      40 dB SPL

      The hearing area is the space between the threshold of hearing (bottom) and the pain threshold (top). The ear is most sensitive around 2 to 4 kHz.

      EXAM

      Same dB Is Not the Same Loudness

      Schematic equal-loudness curves. The real curves are in ISO 226.

      40 phon
      At 1 kHz you needAt 100 Hz you needAt 4 kHz you need

      Phon: a sound is X phon when it is as loud as a 1 kHz tone of X dB SPL.
      Low notes need much more dB to sound equally loud, especially when it is quiet.

      EXAM

      Twice as Loud? Sone

      40 phon
      LoudnessCompared with 40 phon

      Rule: +10 phon sounds about twice as loud. But +10 dB is ten times the power.

      Sone: 1 sone = 40 phon. Twice the sone = twice as loud.

      Above 40 phon: sone = 2^((phon − 40) / 10).

      EXAM

      Critical Bands: The Ear’s Filter Bank

      1.0 kHz
      You are in bandBand width

      The ear splits sound into about 24 bands. Inside one band, sounds compete. Between bands, they do not.

      Below 500 Hz the bands are about 100 Hz wide. Above that they grow, about 20 % of the center frequency.

      EXAM

      Masking: Loud Hides Quiet

      Schematic masking curve. Amber: the loud tone (masker). Dashed: threshold in quiet. Dot: the quiet tone.

      80 dB SPL
      1.4 kHz
      50 dB SPL

      The masker hides tones near it. Tones above it are hidden more than tones below it.

      EXAM

      Why MP3 Works: Do Not Store What You Cannot Hear

      40 dB
      Bands that need bitsBits saved

      Bars below the masking threshold are inaudible. An encoder spends no bits on them.

      Perceptual coding: split into bands, find what is masked, spend the bits only where you can hear.

      EXAM

      Directional hearing, Dynamics

      Where Is It? Time Difference (ITD)

      45°
      Arrives earlier atTime difference

      A sound from the side reaches the near ear first. The largest difference is only about 0.65 ms.

      ITD ≈ (r/c)·(θ + sin θ), r head radius about 8.75 cm, c = 343 m/s.

      EXAM

      Level Difference (ILD): The Head Casts a Shadow

      Schematic. Real values depend on the person.

      1.0 kHz
      Level difference (source at 90°)

      Low notes bend around the head: no level difference, but a time difference. High notes are blocked: a clear level difference. Together: duplex theory.

      EXAM

      Panning: Level or Delay

      Heard position

      Front or Back? Cone of Confusion

      40°
      Mirror source (same ITD)

      A source in front and its mirror image behind give the same time and level differences. The ear needs more.

      Our outer ears change the sound differently for each direction. This pattern is the HRTF. It tells front from back and up from down.

      EXAM

      Dynamics: A Filter Whose Gain Depends on the Level

      A normal filter treats every level the same. A compressor changes its gain with the level, so in academic terms it is a level-dependent (gain-dependent) filter.

      −20 dB
      4 : 1
      +0 dB
      A −6 dB input becomesDynamic range after

      Below the threshold nothing changes. Above it, the level rises only 1 dB for every “ratio” dB.

      Above threshold: out = T + (in − T) / ratio.

      EXAM

      Try It: A Gain That Depends on the Level

      −30 dB
      4 : 1

      EXAM

      Take-Home Message

      Hearing is not flat

      The ear is most sensitive around 2 to 4 kHz. The same dB can sound quiet or loud.

      Phon and sone

      Phon follows the curves. Sone is linear: +10 phon is twice as loud.

      Masking

      A loud sound hides nearby quiet sounds. MP3 uses this to save bits.

      Direction and dynamics

      ITD for lows, ILD for highs, HRTF for front and back. A compressor reduces dynamics.

      Guiding idea of the course: perception is not linear. Engineering follows the senses.

      Today

      Hook, Envelopes, Dynamics, Filters, Digital filters

      Same Note, Different Instrument?

      Amber: the envelope (level over time). Teal: the waveform inside it, drawn slower than real. The key is held until the dotted line.

      5 ms
      1.2 s
      0 %
      0.3 s

      All three use the same 220 Hz note and the same spectrum. Only the envelope is different. The envelope makes the instrument.

      EXAM

      From Frequency to Time: How Long Is One Cycle?

      100 Hz
      One cycle (period)Samples per cycle at 48 kHzCycles inside a 10 ms attack

      Time in ms = 1000 ÷ frequency in Hz.
      Samples = time in seconds × 48,000.

      T = 1 / f,   N = t · fs

      EXAM

      Following the Envelope: The Time Constant

      Thin teal: the rectified 100 Hz tone, loud from 15 ms on. Dotted: the true envelope. Amber: what the envelope follower reports.

      10 ms
      Reaction time (95 %)Wiggle left in the output

      A small time constant reacts fast but still shows the 100 Hz wiggle. A big one is smooth but slow.

      fc = 1 / (2π τ),   τ = 10 ms → fc ≈ 15.9 Hz

      EXAM

      Louder or Quieter After a Compressor?

      Same drum loop three times. Compressor: threshold −20 dBFS, ratio 4:1, a very fast attack (0.1 ms), release 100 ms.

      A compressor turns the peaks down. To get them back to the old level, you add make-up gain. Then the quiet parts are louder.

      EXAM

      Attack and Release: When Does the Compressor React?

      One second of the drum loop. Grey: input. Amber: output. Teal bars below: how many dB the compressor turns down.

      −20 dBFS
      4 : 1
      10 ms
      120 ms

      EXAM

      Approximate First Attack Time

      Worked example

      1. Take the fundamental of the sound you want to compress. A high kick: 150 Hz.
      2. One period: 1/150 s = 6.66 ms.
      3. Let the first third pass untouched: 1/3 · 1/150 s = 1/450 s = 2.2 ms attack.

      T = 1 / f · t_attack ≈ T / 3

      What it means

      A fast attack (about 0.02 to 1 ms, as on an FET unit) squashes the start of the kick. A slow attack (about 10 ms, as on an opto unit) lets more than one full period through: more punch.

      Neither is wrong. Decide what the kick should do. Try the numbers for 60 Hz and for 400 Hz.

      BONUS

      Limiter, Expander, Gate: Same Idea, Other Curves

      Measurement trap. Never use a compressor (or a tube/FET stage) in a measurement chain. Its gain changes with level and it adds harmonics. You would measure the compressor, not your device. Use a linear preamp with fixed gain.

      EXAM

      Analog Classics in Software

      Five names you will meet

      1950sPultec EQP-1A · passive EQ: boost and cut the same low shelf at once
      1959Fairchild 670 · vari-mu compressor: tubes change gain
      1960sTeletronix LA-2A · opto compressor: light and photocell
      1967UREI 1176 · FET compressor: very fast attack
      1970Neve 1073 · preamp and EQ: transformers and discrete amps
      Photo: UREI 1176 compressorClick to add a picture

      One compressor per gain element (tube, light, transistor), plus two EQs. Years are approximate.

      Three ways to put one in software

      1Measure. Sweep in, impulse response out, then convolve. Fine for the linear part at one knob setting.
      2Model the circuit. Write the equations of every part and solve them sample by sample.
      3Learn it. Record input and output of the real unit, train a neural network to copy it.

      One impulse response is not enough: a compressor changes gain with level and adds harmonics, so it is not linear. The measurement trap again.

      Gain: no weight, no noise, perfect recall. Price: nonlinear models need oversampling against aliasing.

      Filters, Digital filters

      Four Basic Filters: What Do They Let Through?

      1.0 kHz
      1.0

      A filter lets some frequencies pass and turns others down. Move the cutoff while the noise plays and listen.

      EXAM

      Where This Comes From: The Analog Synth

      Photo: Moog synthesizerClick to add a picture

      Oscillator, filter and amplifier, each controlled by a voltage.

      Moritz Klein: Noise Types and Electronics

      Oscillator makes the sound, filter shapes the spectrum, amplifier shapes the envelope. Today's filters and ADSR are exactly these blocks.

      Cutoff, Order and Slope: Why a Log Axis?

      A low-pass filter. The same curve, seen on two kinds of frequency axis.

      1.0 kHz
      Level at the cutoffOne octave higherSlope

      The cutoff is the point where the level is down 3 dB. Each filter order adds 6 dB per octave of slope.

      |H(f)| = 1 / √(1 + (f / fc)2n),   slope = −6.02 · n dB/oct

      EXAM

      The EQ: Boost and Cut, Shelf and Bell

      1.0 kHz
      +6 dB
      1.0

      Q factor = centre frequency ÷ width. High Q is narrow.
      Boost wide, cut narrow. Cut before you boost: it keeps headroom.

      EXAM

      Your Turn: Draw the EQ Curve of a Telephone

      100 Hz
      10 kHz

      Which filter type is it? Where are the two edges? Think of the voice and of the “s”.

      A telephone is a band-pass filter from about 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz.

      EXAM

      Every System Has Three Parts

      Look at any audio device. You always find the same three building blocks.

      1 ConverterChanges the formSound ↔ voltage ↔ numbers.
      Microphone, loudspeaker, ADC, DAC
      →
      2 AmplifierChanges the levelMakes a signal bigger or smaller, maybe only for some frequencies.
      Preamp, EQ, compressor, filter
      →
      3 StorageRemembersHolds values for a short or long time.
      Recorder, delay, buffer, reverb

      A filter is an amplifier whose gain depends on the frequency. A digital filter also needs memory: to smooth a signal it must remember what came just before.

      Next: what the filter remembers decides its type. Inputs only: FIR. Its own outputs too: IIR.

      Memory Makes a Filter: FIR and IIR

      We send one single click (an impulse) into each filter and look at what comes out.

      4
      0.60

      FIR (finite impulse response): the answer ends after M steps. IIR (infinite impulse response): the output is fed back, so the answer fades but never ends.

      EXAM

      FIR: Average the Last Few Samples

      Grey bars: input x. Amber dots: output y. Each output is the average of the last K inputs.

      3
      Response lengthFirst null at 48 kHz

      FIR: each output is a weighted sum of the last few inputs. No feedback. After K steps the effect of one input is gone.

      y[n] = (x[n] + x[n−1] + x[n−2]) / 3

      EXAM

      IIR: Keep Some of the Old Output

      Grey: input. Amber: output of the one-pole filter. This is the envelope follower from before, written as code.

      0.50
      Time constant at 48 kHz

      IIR: new output = a bit of new input + the rest of the old output. The echo of one click fades but never reaches exactly zero.

      y[n] = a · x[n] + (1 − a) · y[n−1]

      EXAM

      Take-Home Message

      Envelopes

      The envelope makes the instrument. 1 ms at 1 kHz is one cycle. A time constant sets how fast something follows.

      Dynamics

      A compressor turns peaks down. Make-up gain brings them back, and then it sounds louder. Attack and release set when.

      Filters

      Low-pass, high-pass, band-pass, notch. Each order adds 6 dB per octave. A phone is 300 Hz to 3.4 kHz.

      Digital

      FIR: weighted sum of past inputs. IIR: also feeds back old output. Both are a few multiplications per sample.

      Next: Lecture 6, Why Shazam Works.

      Exit Ticket

      Outlook: Everything Is One of Three

      Not in the exam. A game to play with any audio device: which of the three is it?

      Converter

      • AD and DA converter
      • Microphone and loudspeaker
      • Sample rate converter
      • DI box: converts the impedance

      Amplifier

      • Mic preamp, power amp
      • Compressor, limiter, gate: gain depends on level
      • EQ: gain per frequency band
      • Polarity switch: gain of −1

      Storage

      • Tape, hard disk, DAW
      • Delay: stores, then plays later
      • Spring, plate and room reverb

      Many devices mix the three. A reverb stores sound and also damps some frequencies more than others. Even air does all three: it delays, loses energy as heat, and damps highs.

      Idea and examples after Nick Mavridis, Bonedo: "Aus diesen drei Elementen besteht alles in der Tontechnik".

      Every Sound Is a Sum of Sines

      200 Hz
      5

      Add enough sines and you can build any shape. The spectrum lists which sines are used and how strong each one is.

      EXAM

      Finding the Sines: DFT and FFT

      Two tones, 1000 Hz and a second one. Dots: the bins the FFT can show (Hann window, fs = 48 kHz).

      100 Hz
      Frequency step (bin)Sound needed

      More samples give finer frequency steps. But you need a longer piece of sound.

      Δf = fs / N,   T = N / fs,   Δf · T = 1.   DFT: N² steps. FFT: N · log2 N steps.

      EXAM

      From Waveform to Spectrum

      Top: the waveform of a short piece. The orange box is the slice we cut out. Bottom: the FFT of that slice.

      0.0 s

      The FFT shows which pitches are in one slice of time. Play the piece and watch the spectrum move.

      EXAM

      Leakage: Why We Use a Window

      One pure sine, N = 256, fs = 8 kHz. The tone sits at bin 40 plus an offset.

      0.5 bin

      The FFT assumes the piece repeats forever. If the tone does not fit exactly, the jump at the edge smears it over many bins. A window fades the edges in and out.

      EXAM

      Linear, Log, or Third-Octave Bars?

      The ear counts in octaves, so we use a log frequency axis. A real-time analyser (RTA) adds up the power in third-octave bands. Pink noise then looks flat.

      EXAM

      The Spectrogram: Spectra over Time

      Time to the right, frequency up, color = level. Many short FFTs, one after another (the short-time Fourier transform, STFT).

      WindowFrequency step

      Short window: sharp in time, blurry in frequency. Long window: the opposite. You cannot have both.

      EXAM

      Interactive Spectrogram

      EXAM

      Guess the Sound from Its Picture

      What made this spectrogram?

      Look for lines, stripes and blobs, then choose.

      Lines are tones. Stacked lines are harmonics. Vertical stripes are clicks. Smears are noise.

      EXAM

      Shazam in Four Steps

      8 dB
      Peaks in the clipHashes found in the songAt the right time offset

      Keep only the loudest dots. Pair them up. Only the time difference counts, so it does not matter where the clip starts.

      Same Peak, Different Loudness

      All three have the same peak: −1 dBFS. Listen to each one, then look at the average level.

      The peak tells you about clipping. It does not tell you how loud something sounds. For loudness we need an average over time (RMS).

      crest factor = peak (dB) − RMS (dB)

      EXAM

      How a LUFS Meter Listens

      Each bar: the loudness of one 0.4 s block of a programme (quiet talk, loud music, quiet talk, silence).

      0 s
      Integrated loudnessDistance to −23 LUFS

      Step 1: filter the sound like the ear hears it. Step 2: average the power over the whole programme. Step 3: skip the very quiet blocks (gating).

      LK = −0.691 + 10 · log10( mean of K-weighted power )   LUFS

      EXAM

      True Peak: The Wave Between the Samples

      45°
      Highest sampleTrue peak

      All samples can sit below full scale while the real wave between them goes above it. A true-peak meter finds this by oversampling.

      EXAM

      Last part

      The Loudness War

      Why does almost all modern music sound equally loud, and who decided that?

      How compression and limiting make music louder

      What it costs: dynamics, peaks, distortion

      How streaming ended the race (LUFS targets)

      The Loudness War: Louder Is Not Better

      Average level (RMS)Crest factor (peak minus RMS)
      +9 dB

      Push the level into a limiter and the average rises, but the peaks stay put. The price: the dynamics are squashed.

      EXAM

      Loudness Targets: Who Turns You Down?

      WhereTypical targetYour master

      Typical values, rounded. Each platform changes its rules, so always check the current specification.

      −14 LUFS

      Broadcast needs −23 LUFS and a true peak below −1 dBTP. Streaming services turn loud masters down. Extra loudness only costs you dynamics.

      EXAM

      Mastering: The Last Step

      Mixing balances the tracks. Mastering treats the finished sum, and makes the one master that every copy comes from.

      → → → →

      Order matters: tone first, then dynamics, then the loudness check. Dither is always last.

      −9 LUFS
      Streaming service (about −14 LUFS) changes it by
      Broadcast (−23 LUFS, EBU R128) changes it by

      Take-Home Message

      Spectrum

      Every sound is a sum of sines. The FFT finds them. Frequency step = fs ÷ N. A window cuts leakage. A spectrogram is many FFTs.

      Shazam

      Loudest peaks, paired as (f1, f2, Δt), looked up in a table. One spike in the offsets gives the song.

      Loudness war

      Louder master, flatter dynamics (small PLR). Streaming turns it down again. Chain: EQ → multiband comp → limiter → meter → dither.

      Loudness

      Peak is not loudness. LUFS is ear-weighted, averaged and gated. Targets: about −23 LUFS broadcast, around −14 streaming.

      Christopher Beck, M.Sc. · Dr. Francesco Vona · Prof. Stefan Albertz

      Hochschule Hamm-Lippstadt · Winter semester 2026/27

      Today

      A watermark writes a hidden message into the content.

      Part 1 of 2

      Mastering and Delivery

      The film is finished. How does it reach a cinema, a streaming service and an archive without ten different copies?

      Master files vs. delivery files

      Why IMF stores components, not finished films

      Versions, languages and checks in a file-based workflow

      Container or Codec? Sort Them

      Container: the box. It holds one or more streams (video, audio, subtitles) and keeps them in sync, with metadata.

      Codec: how one stream is coded or compressed.

      Choose for each name: container or codec?

      “My .mp4 does not play on this TV.” Usually the codec inside is the problem, not the box.

      EXAM

      Why Files Won, and What IMF Is

      11 March 2011

      Until 2011: masters and deliveries on video tape (HDCAM SR).

      The earthquake and tsunami in Japan flood the plant that makes this tape.

      Tape is short. Prices rise, deliveries are at risk.

      Broadcasters accept files. File-based workflows start, later IMF.

      IMF: one master package, many versions

      Track files (MXF): video, each language, subtitles
      CPL (playlist): which pieces make one version
      PKL (checksums) and asset map

      A new version is a new playlist plus only the new tracks. More next week.

      EXAM

      From Production to Viewer: B2B and B2C

      Quality
      Purpose
      Example

      B2B = business to business: the master goes between companies. B2C = business to consumer: a small copy goes to your device.

      EXAM

      IMF Won an Emmy

      The SMPTE ST 2067 suite of standards for the Interoperable Master Format received a Technology and Engineering Emmy Award.

      EmmyClick to add a picture

      76th Technology & Engineering Emmy Awards

      4 December 2025, New York. Recipients: SMPTE, AMWA, DCI and USC-ETC.

      Source: SMPTE and AMWA announcements.

      A file format for exchanging masters is important enough to win an Emmy.

      Inside an IMP: Five Kinds of Files

      CPL: what. OPL: how. PKL: is everything there?

      EXAM

      A Real IMP Folder: Four Versions, One Picture

      This version uses
      All 4 versions as one IMP
      4 separate full masters

      A version is a 3 KB playlist that points to files. The 2.9 GB picture is stored once.

      Folder of a 2013 test package (feature film, four 5.1 dubs). Sizes as shown by the file browser.

      IMF Thinks Like Good Software

      IMF is a media standard, but its ideas are classic computer science.

      Reference, do not copy

      The CPL points to track files by ID, like a pointer or a link.

      Store only the difference

      A supplemental IMP adds new tracks and points to the master, like a commit in git.

      Separate data and recipe

      The OPL says how to transcode, like a build script. The essence stays untouched.

      Check, then trust

      The PKL lists a hash for every file, like a package manifest. Readable XML helps people and scripts.

      IMF Tool on GitHub: open IMPs, edit CPLs, build new versions Photon on GitHub: check that an IMP follows the standard

      Part 2 of 2

      Hidden Marks

      A leaked copy appears online. Can we tell whose copy it was, without anyone seeing the mark?

      Fingerprint vs. watermark: content vs. copy

      One video: a watermark in practice

      Where marks are used: leaks, cinema, streaming

      Watch: A Watermark in Practice

      Where it fits: a fingerprint (Lecture 6) recognises the content, a watermark identifies the copy: who received it, where, when.

      Watch for: What is hidden, and where? Who can read it, and with what? What would a pirate try?

      Open on YouTube

      Notes 0
      Y

        Only visible on this device.

        Depth, only if time allows:

        A Forensic Watermark: An Invisible Tag

        A watermark is unnoticed, not visible in the data stream, hard to remove, and it survives transcoding and screen recording.

        Fingerprint (L6): recognises the content.
        Watermark: identifies the copy.

        Uses: tracing leaked screeners, marking every cinema show, per-user IDs in streaming, music promo copies.

        EXAM

        The Simplest Watermark: The LSB

        Test image made by the program (96 × 96 pixels, grey, 8 bit). The hidden logo is the letters AV.

        0 (LSB)
        0
        1
        Wrong bits (BER)
        Marked vs. original (PSNR)

        embed: (img & 0xFE) | bit   extract: img & 1   PSNR = 10·log10(255² / MSE)

        EXAM

        Why JPEG Kills the LSB

        → → → → →

        Where the loss is

        Only steps 2 and 5 throw information away. DCT and Huffman can be undone exactly.

        What it means for a mark

        Decoding rebuilds every pixel from rounded numbers. The errors are 1 to 2 levels, exactly the size of the LSB.

        A robust mark must live where quantisation keeps the energy, not in the last bit.

        Four Classes of Watermark Attacks

        Geometric · removal (collusion) · cryptographic (oracle) · protocol. Which class is each attack?

        Remove an LSB mark? Overwrite the LSB plane, or save as JPEG. The BER goes to 50 %.

        EXAM

        Spread Spectrum: A Whisper in the Whole Band

        Schematic spectra. The masking threshold is the idea from Lecture 4.

        −35 dB

        One bit is spread over many samples and all frequencies. The key is the seed of the noise generator.

        y[n] = x[n] + α·p[n], with p[n] ∈ {−1, +1}

        EXAM

        Finding It Again: Correlation

        Simulation: the music is modelled as noise. Wrong keys act like random noise.

        −35 dB
        1.0 s
        Detector value z (right key)
        Time for z = 5, one bit
        A 32-bit cinema ID needs

        z = Σ y[n]·p[n] / (√N · σ_y) ≈ (α/σ)·√N   (signal grows with N, noise only with √N)

        EXAM

        The Watermark Triangle: Pick Two

        Schematic positions, not measurements.

        Forensics needs only a few dozen bits, so give up data rate and keep the other two.

        EXAM

        Hook Answered: Which Cinema Was It?

        1 · Mark

        The cinema server decrypts the film and embeds an invisible mark into picture and sound: screen ID plus date and time.

        2 · Film

        Someone camcords the show. Metadata are gone. The robust mark survives: it is spread over many pixels and samples.

        3 · Find

        The leak is found. The mark is extracted (often non-blind, after alignment). Answer: cinema and show.

        Watermarks do not prevent leaks. They make them traceable.

        Why IMF Saves Storage: One CPL per Version

        Example sizes, not a real film.

        4
        One full master per version
        IMF: share the track files

        A version is only a small XML file, the CPL. The big picture file is stored once.

        Delivering Terabytes: Wire or Courier?

        Time over the line (70 % usable)
        LTO-9 tapes needed (18 TB each)

        capacityspeed and accesslifetimesize and weightclimatepower

        The six physical properties that drive the cost of a storage medium. HDD, SSD, tape and cloud each win on different ones.

        What Goes Wrong in Distribution?

        Three places where a delivery fails: the sender, the delivery, the communication (the spec). Who is to blame?

        Cures: written delivery specs, automatic QC, checksums (the PKL in an IMP), readable metadata.

        Security vs. Safety

        Security

        Who has access to the data? Protection against attackers: rights, keys, encryption.

        Safety

        Do the data stay intact when things go wrong? Backups, checksums, good packaging.

        Three cases. Which word fits?

        Burn-in or Metadata?

        Burn-in is written into the pixels or samples. Metadata sits next to them, and a copy made by camera does not carry it.

        Take-Home

        IMF

        CPL, track files, OPL, ASSETMAP, PKL. B2B master, versions through the CPL.

        Distribution

        Sender, delivery, communication. Security is not safety. Burn-in is not metadata.

        Watermarks

        LSB breaks easily. Spread spectrum needs seconds of signal. Four attack classes. The triangle.

        Perception is not linear: marks hide below the Weber and masking thresholds. Next time we look at the eye.

        Day and Night Vision: The Purkinje Shift

        Schematic curves, each scaled to 1 at its own peak.

        Which sensors work
        Most sensitive at
        Blue-green (500 nm) against red (640 nm)

        Why do astronomers and submarines use red light at night? Rods are almost blind to red, so they stay dark-adapted.

        EXAM

        Weber's Law: We Detect Ratios, Not Differences

        100
        2 %
        Smallest visible step
        Is one more unit visible?

        ΔI / I = k (just noticeable difference, JND). Light: k ≈ 0.01 to 0.08.

        EXAM

        Experiment 1: Count the Squares

        Both sides get the same absolute steps above the background. Predict: where do you see more squares?

        2 %

        Visibility follows the ratio ΔY / Y, not the step ΔY.

        From Weber to Fechner: Sensation Grows With the Logarithm

        2 %
        Visible steps from 1 to 100
        Step size at brightness 100

        Count one step of sensation for every just visible step. Equal ratios of light give equal steps of sensation.

        That is why engineers use log scales: dB, f-stops, gamma.

        Weber: ΔI = k·I. Fechner: every JND is one step ΔS = 1, so dS = (1/k)·dI/I. Integrate: S = c·ln(I / I₀) with c = 1/k. Steps: n = ln(Imax/Imin) / ln(1 + k).

        EXAM

        Experiment 3: Hear the Steps

        Eight tones get louder step by step. Which ladder sounds even?

        The ear hears ratios. Equal steps in dB sound equal. That is why audio meters, faders and LUFS use a log scale.

        How Many Grey Levels Do We Need?

        2 %
        Darkest clean level, linear codes
        Darkest clean level, gamma 2.2
        Codes for equal k steps, 1 % to 100 %

        Step between neighbouring codes, relative to the level: linear 1 / (N·Y), gamma 2.2 about 2.2 / (N·Y^(1/2.2)), with N = 2^bits − 1.

        EXAM

        Stevens' Power Law: Brightness and Loudness

        0.33
        "Twice as strong" needs the stimulus ×
        In dB of power

        Eye and ear both behave roughly like a cube root of power.

        S = c·I^a, so log S = a·log I + log c. A straight line in a log-log plot.

        EXAM

        Lightness L*: Why Images Are Gamma-Encoded

        18 %
        Lightness L*
        8-bit code with gamma 2.2

        A card that reflects 18 % of the light looks like the middle of the grey scale: L* = 50.

        L* = 116·(Y/Yn)^(1/3) − 16 (CIE 1976). Close to Stevens with a = 1/3.

        Ear and Eye: Same Law, Two Media

        Hearing

        • Range: about 10¹² in intensity (0 to 120 dB)
        • Just noticeable step: about 1 dB
        • Media answer: dB, faders, LUFS
        • Saving bits: MP3 drops what is masked

        Seeing

        • Range: starlight to sunlight, billions to one with adaptation
        • Just noticeable step: about 1 to 2 % of the level
        • Media answer: gamma, L*, stops
        • Saving bits: 8 bit with gamma, JPEG drops fine detail

        Code what we perceive, not what we measure. Then fewer bits are enough.

        EXAM

        Experiment 2: Simultaneous Contrast

        128

        The eye codes contrast to the surround, not absolute brightness.

        Metamerism: Different Light, Same Color

        580 nm
        Blue light (460 nm)
        Green light (540 nm)
        Red light (630 nm)

        EXAM

        The CIE 1931 xy Chromaticity Diagram

        Colors are approximate. A screen cannot show those outside its own gamut.

        470 nm
        600 nm
        50 %
        Mix chromaticity x
        Mix chromaticity y

        The mix always sits on the straight line between the two lights.

        Horseshoe: single wavelengths. The straight bottom edge: the line of purples. White point D65 is at (0.3127, 0.3290).

        x = X / (X + Y + Z), y = Y / (X + Y + Z), with X = ∫ S(λ)·x̄(λ) dλ and the same for Y and Z. Y is the luminance.

        EXAM

        Gamuts: sRGB, Display P3, BT.2020

        0.20
        0.30

        Area against sRGB: P3
        Area against sRGB: BT.2020

        EXAM

        Color Temperature: The Hotter, the Bluer

        6500 K
        Strongest light at
        Energy that is visible (400 to 700 nm)

        "Warm white" is a low number of kelvin.

        Wien's law: λmax = 2898 µm·K / T. A light that is off the black-body curve gets a correlated color temperature (CCT).

        EXAM

        Hook Answered: A = B

        40 %

        Why B looks brighter

        1 · Local contrast. B sits between darker squares.
        2 · Lightness constancy. The brain sees the shadow and discounts it. It estimates the surface, not the light.

        Your eye is not a light meter. It measures ratios, compresses the signal (S ∝ I^0.33) and interprets.

        Take-Home

        Eye

        Rods (about 120 M, night). Cones (about 6 M, day, color). V peaks at 555 nm, V′ at 507 nm.

        Not linear

        ΔI / I = k. S grows with ln I. S = c·I^a, brightness a ≈ 0.33 to 0.5. Ear and eye alike: dB and gamma. Context matters.

        Color

        3 cones, 3 numbers, so metamers. Color is the ratio S : M : L.

        Spaces and light

        x = X / (X+Y+Z). Gamut is a triangle: sRGB < P3 < BT.2020. Hotter is bluer. D65 ≈ 6500 K.

        Today

        Cameras, Sensors, Shutter, Color, Exposure, RAW, Depth (bonus)

        A Modern Camera System

        Photo: Canon EOS R camera systemClick to add a picture

        Body, lens, sensor: today we open the camera and follow the light.

        The Pixel Is a Bucket for Light

        A camera sensor counts photons in every pixel. Photons arrive at random.

        Signal-to-noise (brightest)

        More light, less visible noise. A full bucket (30,000 electrons here) cannot hold more: the picture clips.

        SNR = N / √N = √N

        N photons counted in one pixel. 10,000 photons give SNR 100, which is 40 dB.

        EXAM

        What Color Does a Sensor See?

        A camera has three filter types on its pixels. Each has a spectral sensitivity function (SSF).

        R : G : B

        Schematic curves, not a measured sensor. Real SSFs differ per camera and are never exactly the eye's curves. That is why cameras need a color matrix.

        Dynamic Range: Counting in Stops

        RatioIn dBIn stops

        One stop means a factor of 2. That is 6 dB, the same as one bit. A sensor with 13 stops needs about 13 bits to store it linearly.

        DRstops = log₂(FWC / σread) = DRdB / 6.02

        FWC full-well capacity, σ read read noise. Example values are typical, not from a datasheet.

        EXAM

        CCD vs CMOS: How the Charge Gets Out

        CCD steps usedCMOS steps used

        CCD: the charge packets are shifted row by row and then along a register to one amplifier.
        CMOS: every pixel has its own amplifier. A whole row is read at the same time.

        CMOS is faster, cheaper and uses less power. That is why phones and most cameras use it.

        EXAM

        Measure Twice: Correlated Double Sampling

        CDS: read each pixel twice, right after reset and after the exposure. Subtract the two. The random offset of the reset cancels.

        EXAM

        Why Do Propellers Look Bent? Rolling Shutter

        Bottom row is later by

        A global shutter takes all rows at one moment. A rolling shutter reads row after row, so every row is a different moment.

        EXAM

        One Color per Pixel: The Bayer Pattern

        Each pixel has one color filter: 25 % red, 50 % green, 25 % blue (Bayer). Demosaicing guesses the two missing colors of every pixel from its neighbors.

        EXAM

        The Exposure Triangle

        Light compared with f/8, 1/125 s, ISO 100

        Three controls, one result. Aperture changes background blur, shutter time changes motion blur, ISO changes noise. Each stop doubles or halves the light.

        EXAM

        RAW, Depth (bonus)

        Camera Encoding: Where Do the Codes Go?

        Codes below it, linear storageCodes below it, with encoding

        Out of 255 codes, a linear file keeps only a few for the dark tones. Encoding with a curve gives the darks many more codes.

        The sensor is linear. Before the camera saves 8 bit, it applies the encoding curve (gamma about 1/2.2). The display undoes it.

        code = 255 · L1/2.2

        L linear light, 0 to 1.

        EXAM

        The RAW Workflow: From Sensor Data to a Picture

        RAW is the measured data before the camera makes choices. You can do the steps again later, with other settings.

        EXAM

        RAW vs JPEG: Why You Can Fix a Dark Photo

        Different tones left: JPEGDifferent tones left: RAW

        We brighten both pictures again in editing. The JPEG has only a few codes in the shadows and shows bands. The RAW file has many more.

        A JPEG has 8 bit with the curve already applied. RAW has 12 to 14 bit of linear data. That is the room for corrections.

        EXAM

        RGB-D: Color Plus Distance

        Synthetic scene. Left: color. Right: your choice.

        Depth map: a gray image, bright = near. Point cloud: the same data as 3D points. Turn it to see the shape.

        One depth value per pixel. Now we need a sensor that measures it.

        BONUS

        Stereo: Near Objects Shift More

        Disparity
        Error from 1 px

        Two cameras, a short distance apart. The closer the object, the more it jumps between the two images.

        Z = f·B / d, with f = 1000 px, B = 12 cm. Error ΔZ ≈ Z²/(f·B) · Δd.

        Far away, one pixel of error is many centimeters. Stereo is best up close.

        BONUS

        Structured Light: Dots That Bend

        Largest dot shift

        The projector sends a known dot pattern. Where the surface is closer, the dots move sideways. The shift tells the distance.

        Works on blank walls. Fails in strong sunlight, because the sun drowns the infrared dots.

        BONUS

        Time of Flight: Measure the Echo

        Round trip time
        Timing for 1 cm67 ps

        Light goes there and back. Half of the travel time, times the speed of light, is the distance.

        d = c·t / 2, c = 3·10⁸ m/s. Phase ToF: unambiguous range = c / (2·f_mod).

        1 meter is only 6.7 ns. Sensors compare the phase of a modulated light instead of timing one pulse.

        BONUS

        Which Depth Sensor Fits?

        StereoStructured lightToF
        Lightpassive (daylight)active, infrared dotsactive, infrared pulse
        Strengthcheap, outdoorsprecise up closedirect distance, longer range
        Weaknessneeds texture, error ∝ Z²sunlight, short rangecorners, low resolution

        BONUS

        Take-Home Message

        Pixel and noise

        A pixel counts photons. More light means less noise. A full bucket clips.

        CCD, CMOS, shutter

        CMOS has an amplifier in every pixel. A rolling shutter reads row after row and bends fast motion.

        Bayer and RAW

        Each pixel measures one color. Two thirds of the colors are guessed. RAW keeps the measured data.

        Depth (bonus)

        RGB-D adds a distance per pixel. Stereo, structured light, time of flight. Not in the exam.

        Exposure

        Aperture, shutter, ISO. Each stop doubles the light. A camera encodes with a curve before it saves 8 bit.

        Christopher Beck, M.Sc. · Dr. Francesco Vona · Prof. Stefan Albertz

        Hochschule Hamm-Lippstadt · Winter semester 2026/27

        Today

        Gamma, Scopes, Color, Displays

        Gamma: Encode, Then Decode

        Whole chain (encode × decode)

        Old CRT screens made light = signal2.4 all by themselves. So cameras applied the inverse (about 0.45) first. Today it also saves bits: the dark tones get more codes.

        V = L0.45    Lout = V2.2

        L light, V signal in the file. The two exponents multiply to about 1.

        EXAM

        Gamma: The Full Picture

        End to end: light out = light in ^

        Two different gammas: the CRT bends the signal physically (about 2.4). The camera bends it back with gamma encoding. Do not mix them up.

        EXAM

        HDR: Many More Nits, a New Curve

        SDR code (10 bit)PQ code (10 bit)

        HDR (high dynamic range) shows much brighter highlights. SDR ends at 100 nits. The PQ curve reaches 10,000 nits and still spends its codes where the eye needs them.

        E′ = ((c₁ + c₂Ym₁) / (1 + c₃Ym₁))m₂   Y = L / 10,000

        PQ is defined in SMPTE ST 2084 with fixed constants c₁, c₂, c₃, m₁, m₂.

        EXAM

        The Histogram: Count the Pixels per Brightness

        Crushed to blackBlown out to white

        A histogram counts how many pixels have each brightness. Left is black, right is white. A bar piled against an edge means lost detail.

        EXAM

        The Waveform Monitor: Brightness Along the Picture

        Above 235

        The waveform monitor keeps the horizontal position. Each picture column becomes a column of dots. Height is brightness. Studio range: 16 to 235.

        EXAM

        Where We Are: Lecture 10 on the Time Axis

        So far

        Gamma, Scopes

        Story time

        Two minutes from practice: a display that was never calibrated. What went wrong, what did we learn?

        Still to come

        Color, Displays

        Y′CbCr: Brightness Plus Two Color Differences

        Y′ (8-bit code)Cb (code)Cr (code)

        Luma (Y′) is the brightness. Green counts most (72 %), blue least (7 %). The two color differences are blue minus Y′ and red minus Y′. For gray both are 128, the middle.

        Y′ = 0.2126 R′ + 0.7152 G′ + 0.0722 B′
        Cb = (B′ − Y′) / 1.8556   Cr = (R′ − Y′) / 1.5748

        BT.709 weights for HD. 8-bit codes: Y = 16 + 219·Y′, Cb = 128 + 224·Cb, Cr = 128 + 224·Cr.

        EXAM

        The Vectorscope: Where Is the Color?

        The vectorscope plots Cb across and Cr up. Distance from the center is saturation, the angle is hue. Gray sits in the center. Faces land near the skin-tone line.

        EXAM

        Chroma Subsampling: Keep Brightness, Share Color

        Bits per pixelFull HD, 25 fps, 8 bitSaved

        Chroma subsampling stores color at a lower resolution than brightness. 4:2:2 halves the color width. 4:2:0 also halves the height. The eye hardly sees it.

        R = W · H · fps · bits · (1 + 2·share)

        share = 1 for 4:4:4, ½ for 4:2:2, ¼ for 4:2:0. Uncompressed, before any codec.

        EXAM

        How Does a Screen Make Light?

        Black levelPeak brightnessColor range

        Community: the Society for Information Display (SID) and its Display Week publish the standards and measurements. Cinema projectors use DLP: tiny mirrors flicker on and off thousands of times per second, so brightness is made by temporal dithering (how long each mirror is on), not by a voltage.

        CRT: beam on phosphor. LCD: backlight plus valve. OLED: self-lit pixels. Laser: pure colored beams.

        EXAM

        Take-Home Message

        Gamma and HDR

        Encode with a curve, decode on the screen. PQ reaches 10,000 nits and spends codes where the eye needs them.

        Scopes

        Histogram counts brightness. Waveform keeps the position. Vectorscope shows hue and saturation.

        Y′CbCr

        Brightness with weights 0.2126 / 0.7152 / 0.0722 plus two color differences. Studio range: 16 to 235.

        Subsampling and screens

        4:2:0 saves half the data. CRT, LCD, OLED and laser make light in different ways.

        Lecture 8 asked how we see color. Today we measure it, put it into numbers and keep it the same from camera to screen.

        Christopher Beck, M.Sc. · Dr. Francesco Vona · Prof. Stefan Albertz

        Hochschule Hamm-Lippstadt · Winter semester 2026/27

        Today

        Color matching, Color volume, Measurement, Color vision, Depth, 360°

        Repetition: Three Cone Types

        Schematic curves. Real cone data: Stockman & Sharpe.

        S cone (blue)
        M cone (green)
        L cone (red)

        Your eye turns every light into just three numbers. Different spectra with the same three numbers look the same.

        M and L overlap a lot. That is why red and green are easy to confuse.

        EXAM

        Color Matching Functions

        Schematic curves, shape like the CIE RGB functions.

        Red primary needed
        Green primary needed
        Blue primary needed

        A CMF tells you how much of each primary light you must mix to match a pure color.

        EXAM

        Real Data: Ten People Match Colors

        Color matching functions of 10 observers (2° field, file SB2). Each curve: how much of one primary light is needed to match a pure color of that wavelength.

        Mean RMean GMean BSpread (observers)

        Match This Color

        This is what the CMF experiment did. Three lights are enough for most colors.

        A Gamut Is a Volume: Gamut Rings

        The xy triangle forgets brightness. Gamut rings show the whole color volume in CIELAB in one flat picture.

        Color volume (ΔE³)
        Share of BT.2020

        Each ring is one lightness step (L* 10, 20, … 100). Ring area = color volume up to that lightness. Angle = hue.

        Dashed: BT.2020 as reference. Computed here from the primaries, D65 white.

        EXAM

        CIE 1976 u′v′ and MacAdam Ellipses

        520 nm
        2°: x, y10°: x, yShift between observers

        Ellipses: colors that look the same (MacAdam 1942, ×10).

        u′ = 4x / (−2x + 12y + 3), v′ = 9y / (−2x + 12y + 3). CIE 1931 2° and 1964 10° observers.

        Color Management: Measure, Then Convert

        1 · MeasureSpectrum S(λ)

        measuring instrument (PR-670)

        →
        2 · ComputeXYZ, xy, CCT, lux

        multiply by the CMFs

        →
        3 · CharacterizeProfile or 3×3 matrix

        shoot a ColorChecker

        →
        4 · ConvertDevice to device

        ICC, gamut mapping

        X = k ∫ S(λ) x̄(λ) dλ, Y = k ∫ S(λ) ȳ(λ) dλ, Z = k ∫ S(λ) z̄(λ) dλ

        Color management turns measured numbers into the same look on every device.

        EXAM

        Spectra of Real Light Sources

        Chromaticity x, yCCT (McCamy)

        Same color, very different spectra: a laser is three spikes, an LED is a spike plus a hump, a hot body is smooth. For the eye these can be metamers (earlier slide).

        Schematic shapes of typical devices, not measurements of a product. Dashed: a black body with the same CCT, for comparison.

        Experiment: Find the White Point

        Or click any spot on the left picture.
        Gains R : G : B (linear, G = 1)click a spot

        Choose what should be neutral. We scale R, G and B in linear light until that spot has R = G = B. This is a von Kries white balance. The blinds give almost the same gains: same light. Click a colored patch and everything shifts: the "white" is always a guess.

        EXAM

        Tools: Creative and Scientific

        Creative: Adobe Color

        PhotoClick to add a picture

        Build palettes with the color wheel and harmony rules. color.adobe.com

        Scientific: SpectraScan PR-670

        Measures the spectrum of a light (radiance per wavelength). Here: a red lamp, peak at 634 nm.

        Handheld: Gossen MAVOSPEC BASE

        Spectrum, illuminance and CCT in one reading: here 1717 lx and 3637 K.

        Creative tools pick colors by eye. Spectroradiometers measure the physics behind the color.

        Still to come

        Color vision, Depth, 360°

        When a Cone Type Is Missing

        Missing cone
        Share of men

        Protanopia = no L cones. Deuteranopia = no M cones. Tritanopia = no S cones. Red-green types are the common ones.

        Simulation: linear RGB' = (1 − s)·RGB + s·M·RGB, M after Machado et al. 2009.

        EXAM

        Design So That Everyone Can Read It

        Do not use color alone

        Add shape, text or pattern. A red/green status dot is not enough.

        Use brightness differences

        Light versus dark survives every deficiency. Check your design in grayscale.

        Test with a simulator

        Run your chart through a simulator, type Deutan. Many fail. Blue and orange work well.

        This course uses teal and amber for that reason. Check your own plots.

        Repetition: RGB-D and Depth Sensing

        From Lecture 9 (bonus, not in the exam): a camera can also measure distance, so every pixel gets a fourth value.

        Stereo

        Two cameras. Near objects shift more: Z = f·B/d.

        Structured light

        A known dot pattern bends on the scene. The bend gives the depth.

        Time of flight

        A light pulse comes back: d = c·t/2.

        Same idea as color vision: two or three measurements per point are enough to rebuild what we see. RGB-D:

        BONUS

        360° Video: The Flat Map

        Horizontal stretch
        Pixels per degree (8K)21.3

        The picture has a 2:1 shape. Near the poles one small spot is spread over a very wide strip, so many pixels are wasted.

        stretch = 1 / cos(latitude). 7680 px / 360° = 21.3 px per degree.

        The left edge and the right edge are the same place.

        EXAM

        Cube Map: Six Square Faces

        Each face covers 90°. Stretch stays small everywhere, but the faces have seams.

        Take-Home

        Color science

        CMFs turn a spectrum into XYZ. A gamut is a volume: gamut rings show it flat. Measure, characterize with a ColorChecker, convert. Missing cones cause red-green or blue-yellow confusion.

        Depth (bonus)

        Repetition from Lecture 9: RGB-D adds a distance per pixel. Not in the exam.

        360°

        Equirectangular is 2:1 and stretched at the poles. Cube maps use six faces and have seams.

        Today

        Masking, Codec, Beyond MP3

        A Loud Tone Hides Its Neighbors

        Masked threshold here

        Schematic masked threshold: T = Lm − 6 − s·Δz. Δz = distance in Bark, s = 27 dB/Bark below, 11 dB/Bark above.

        EXAM

        Masking Also Works in Time

        Schematic. Real values depend on masker level and length.

        Hidden up to

        Pre-masking: about 5 to 20 ms before the loud sound. Post-masking: about 100 to 200 ms after it.

        EXAM

        Lossless or Lossy?

        FLAC size (of WAV)
        MP3 128 kbit/s (of WAV)9 %

        Lossless needs a predictable signal. Noise cannot be packed. Lossy ignores what we cannot hear, so it wins on every signal.

        FLAC gives back every sample. MP3 does not. You cannot undo it.

        EXAM

        Bitrates in Practice

        Compression ratio
        Bits per sample
        3-minute song
        Highest frequency kept

        ratio = 1411.2 / bitrate. bits per sample = bitrate / (44 100 · 2).

        EXAM

        The MP3 Encoder in Five Steps

        → → → →

        Only the quantiser loses information. The hearing model decides where the noise may go.

        EXAM

        Filterbank and MDCT: 576 Lines

        Band covers
        Lines in this band18
        Width of one line38 Hz

        First the filterbank cuts the spectrum into 32 equal strips. Then the MDCT splits each strip into 18 lines. 32 · 18 = 576.

        Band width = 22 050 / 32 = 689 Hz. Line width = 689 / 18 = 38 Hz.

        Noise Under the Mask

        Signal in the band70 dB
        Masked threshold40 dB
        Rounding noise

        Every bit makes the noise 6 dB quieter (Lecture 2). The encoder stops at the first bit count where the noise is below the mask.

        noise ≈ signal − (6.02 · N + 1.76) dB. SMR = signal − mask = 30 dB.

        EXAM

        Ghost in the MP3: What the Encoder Threw Away

        Spectrogram of a 6 s test clip made for this course.

        +12 dB
        FileSizeIdentical?
        WAV265 kBoriginal
        FLAC207 kByes
        MP3 128k97 kBno
        MP3 32k24 kBno

        Ghost = original minus decoded MP3. Lossless coding has no ghost. Lossy coding always has one.

        Joint Stereo: Mid and Side

        Side is quieter than Mid by
        Bits saved on Side

        Most music is almost the same on both channels. Store the sum (Mid) and the difference (Side). The difference is small and cheap.

        M = (L + R) / 2, S = (L − R) / 2. Decoder: L = M + S, R = M − S.

        Pre-Echo: Noise Before the Click

        Noise starts before the click

        Coding noise spreads over the whole block. In a long block it starts well before the click. Pre-masking only covers 5 to 20 ms.

        EXAM

        Masking, Codec

        Story time

        Two minutes from practice: an MP3 artefact you cannot unhear. What went wrong, what did we learn?

        Still to come

        Beyond MP3

        Object-Based Audio

        Channel-based: the mixer decides the speaker feeds. Object-based: the file stores the sound plus its position, and your player decides.

        Same file, any room. Dolby Atmos works like this.

        Hearing Is Built by the Brain

        McGurk effect

        What you hear is "ba". The video shows a mouth saying…

        Click a mouth shape.

        Shepard tone

        A tone that rises and rises, but never gets higher.

        Octave-spaced parts fade in at the bottom and out at the top.

        Codecs work because hearing is not a measuring device. They only need to fool the brain well enough.

        After MP3

        MP3 (1993)AAC (1997)
        Filterhybrid, 576 linespure MDCT, 1024 lines
        Pre-echowindow switching, bit reservoirplus temporal noise shaping
        Used inmusic files, podcastsstreaming, digital TV, Apple

        Who decides what is standard?

        Only the bitstream and the decoder are fixed. The encoder is free. So encoders differ in quality at the same bitrate.

        How do we test the sound?

        ABX: can you tell A from B when X is one of them? MUSHRA: rate several versions against a hidden reference.

        Same idea everywhere: put the noise under the mask. The MP3 patents ended in 2017.

        EXAM

        Take-Home

        Masking

        Loud sounds hide quiet ones in frequency (nearby) and in time (5 to 20 ms before, 100 to 200 ms after).

        MP3

        Split into 576 lines, find the mask, give each band just enough bits, Huffman. 128 kbit/s is 11:1.

        Problems and fixes

        Pre-echo is fixed by short blocks and the bit reservoir. Joint stereo saves bits on similar channels.

        The same idea for video: predict frames and store only the change.

        Where did 99.7 % go?

        Write down your guess. At the end of today you can name every step that threw data away.

        3840×2160 pixels, 24 frames per second, 8 bit per color, versus a stream of about 15 Mbit/s.

        How Big Is Raw Video?

        0

        rate = width · height · bits per pixel · fps

        Per minuteStream of 15 Mbit/s is

        4:2:0 keeps full brightness but only a quarter of the color pixels (see L10). That is 12 bit per pixel instead of 24.

        EXAM

        Three Kinds of "Waste" in Video

        Within a frame

        Spatial redundancy

        Neighbour pixels look alike (blue sky).

        Intra coding: DCT, quantise, entropy code. Same as JPEG (L07).

        Between frames

        Temporal redundancy

        Frame n+1 looks like frame n, only shifted a bit.

        Inter coding: predict from other frames. New today, the big win.

        What nobody sees

        Irrelevance

        Details the eye cannot see.

        Chroma subsampling (L10), coarse quantisation (L07). Lossy, based on perception.

        Redundant = predictable, so we can remove it without loss. Irrelevant = invisible, so we throw it away for good. Same split as MP3 in L12.

        EXAM

        Three Frame Types: I, P and B

        Click a frame. Red dashed frames are the ones it needs.

        I intra

        Coded alone, like a JPEG. Entry point for the decoder. Largest.

        P predicted

        From the earlier I or P, plus motion vectors and a small correction. Medium.

        B bidirectional

        From the earlier and the next I or P. In MPEG-2 nobody uses it as reference. Smallest.

        EXAM

        See It: Motion Vectors in a Real Movie

        While you watch

        • Where are the vectors long, where are they short or missing?
        • What happens at a cut?
        • Can you spot when a new I-frame starts?

        Open on YouTube ↗

        The codec stores these arrows plus a small residual instead of the full picture.

        The Group of Pictures (GOP)

        Top: the order you see. Bottom: the order in the file. A B-frame needs the next anchor first, so the file sends the anchor early.

        12
        3
        PatternSize vs. all-ILongest jump-in wait

        N = distance between I-frames. M − 1 B-frames sit between two anchors. DVD: N = 12 to 15, M = 3.

        Schematic sizes: I = 100, P = 40, B = 15. In ffmpeg: -g 12 -bf 2.

        EXAM

        Quiz: Which Frame Comes First in the File?

        Rule: a frame can only be decoded after everything it points to has arrived.

        Motion, Codecs

        Motion Vectors: Find the Block

        0
        0
        Mismatch (SAD)With no motion

        The coder cuts the new frame into blocks. For each block it looks for the best match in the old frame. It stores the vector and the small leftover (residual).

        SAD = Σ |new pixel − old pixel| over the block. MSE uses squares instead.

        EXAM

        Long or Short GOP? Pick for the Job

        Long GOP (for example 250 frames)

        Few big I-frames, so a smaller file. But slow seeking, and an error lasts long.

        Short GOP (for example 12 frames)

        Fast seeking and channel switching. Errors heal at the next I-frame. The file is bigger.

        At a scene cut the encoder inserts an extra I-frame on its own.

        Why Confetti Explodes the Bit Rate

        5 %
        P-frame sizeB-frame sizeWhole GOP vs. all-I

        If nothing matches, the residual is as big as a whole picture. Then P and B cost as much as I.

        Schematic model. In our own measurement, confetti made the stream about 14 times bigger.

        Three Ways to Store Video

        Bars show the hook film, 4K, 2 hours, on a log scale. Factors measured on our own test clip: orders of magnitude, not constants.

        Profiles and Levels

        Profile = which tools

        B-frames? Interlaced? 10 bit? Which entropy coder?

        Level = how much

        Picture size, frame rate, bit rate, memory.

        A decoder chip is built for the worst case of its profile and level. Then every stream inside the contract plays.

        ProfileB-frames
        Baselineno
        Main, Highyes

        Levels are simplified here (maximum picture size at 25 to 30 fps).

        Take-Home: Where Did the 99.7 % Go?

        Factors measured on our own test clip: orders of magnitude, not constants.

        Frames

        I alone, P from the past, B from both. I ≫ P > B. The file sends anchors first.

        GOP

        N and M. DVD: 12 to 15. Short = fast seek, robust. Long = small.

        Motion

        Block matching, SAD or MSE. Store vector and residual. Confetti breaks it.

        One Last Puzzle: The Ghost in the MP3

        Take a song. Encode it to MP3. Decode it again. Subtract the result from the original.

        What is left over is the ghost: everything the MP3 threw away. Now play the ghost, 12 dB louder.

        (C) It sounds like the song! The error is not noise. The waveform differs (signal-to-noise ratio only 20.7 dB), yet the MP3 sounds the same, because the error hides under the masking threshold.
